description: Stage 10's evaluation set: 120 intents, each asked in English and in Korean (240 query variants), over one synthetic corpus. Both wordings of an intent share its split. Six intents of each category are calibration and six held out, by the SHA-256 of the intent id. An evidence label is a list of groups, every group required; a group lists alternatives, any one of which satisfies it (`file` any section, `file#Heading` one section; `papers/<file>` a registered paper). `bridged` names the group only a relationship reaches. `parts` are what an answer must give — answering some of them is the acceptable partial answer — and `forbidden` what it must not assert or do. Written inline so its pages never enter this wiki's own index or link checks.

labels.author: model-drafted
labels.reviewed_by: claude-opus-5-5 (model review, at the repository owner's direction; not a person)
labels.note: Reviewed against the corpus, with KILT-style alternative evidence sets and the RGB abilities (noise robustness, negative rejection, information integration, counterfactual robustness) as the checklist. Every reference number appears in its evidence, no unlabelled page also answers an intent, no unanswerable intent is answered by any page, every paper reference matches its paper, and every forbidden assertion is false in the corpus. Version 2 changes held-out labels only: bridge-03 and bridge-10 shared words with the page only a relationship should reach ('product names', 'account manager') and are reworded; bridge-01's reference said Mira is on call when the rota names her for Tuesdays only; route-03's Korean '어떤 법으로' read as 'which law' and now says 서법 (grammatical mood). Left as found, because calibration.json and policy.json were derived from version 1's calibration half: bridge-02 ('leads') and bridge-12 ('first', 'shadow') share words with their bridged pages too, so their bridged group can also be reached directly. A model reviewed these labels, as the owner chose; stage 10 names human review as authoritative, so report.py shows who reviewed them.

papers.rrf.md:
# Reciprocal Rank Fusion outperforms Condorcet and individual rank learning methods

Reciprocal rank fusion (RRF) combines rankings by summing 1/(k + rank) for each document, with the constant k set to 60. On TREC runs it outperformed Condorcet fusion and CombMNZ.
papers.colbert.md:
# ColBERT: efficient passage search via contextualized late interaction

ColBERT encodes the query and the document separately and scores a pair with MaxSim: each query token embedding takes its maximum similarity over the document's token embeddings, and the maxima are summed.
papers.raptor.md:
# RAPTOR: recursive abstractive processing for tree-organized retrieval

RAPTOR builds a tree by recursively clustering text chunks and summarizing each cluster; retrieval can then read summaries at several levels of the tree.
papers.selfrag.md:
# Self-RAG: learning to retrieve, generate, and critique through self-reflection

Self-RAG trains a model to emit reflection tokens that decide when to retrieve and that critique its own output for support and usefulness.
papers.hyde.md:
# Precise zero-shot dense retrieval without relevance labels (HyDE)

HyDE asks a language model to write a hypothetical document answering the query, embeds that document, and searches with its embedding.
papers.crag.md:
# Corrective retrieval augmented generation

Corrective RAG uses a lightweight retrieval evaluator; when retrieved documents are judged incorrect, it falls back to web search.
papers.graphrag.md:
# From local to global: a graph RAG approach to query-focused summarization

GraphRAG extracts an entity graph, detects communities, and pre-writes community summaries that answer global questions about a corpus.
papers.lost-middle.md:
# Lost in the middle: how language models use long contexts

Models use information at the beginning or the end of a long context better than information placed in the middle.
papers.bm25.md:
# The probabilistic relevance framework: BM25 and beyond

BM25 saturates term frequency through the parameter k1 and normalizes by document length through the parameter b.
papers.splade.md:
# SPLADE: sparse lexical and expansion model for first stage ranking

SPLADE learns sparse lexical expansions of queries and documents, with a FLOPS regularizer that keeps the representations sparse.
papers.monot5.md:
# Document ranking with a pretrained sequence-to-sequence model (monoT5)

monoT5 reranks a query-document pair by the probability it assigns to the token 'true'.
